ARTICLE: Mental health
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{short description|Level of psychological well-being}}
{{for|mental disorders|Mental disorder}}

[[File:Psi with Rod of Asclepius.svg|thumb|The Greek glyph "'''ψ'''" or "psi" when Latinized, is a common symbol for mental health and well being]]
{{Mental health sidebar}}
{{Public health sidebar|expanded=all}}

'''Mental health''' encompasses [[emotion]]al, [[Psychology|psychological]], and [[Social psychology|social]] [[well-being]], influencing [[cognition]], [[perception]], and [[behavior]].<ref name="mentalhealth.gov">{{Cite web |title=What Is Mental Health? |url=https://www.mentalhealth.gov/basics/what-is-mental-health |access-date=2022-09-22 |website=www.mentalhealth.gov}}</ref> Mental health plays a crucial role in an individual's daily life when managing [[Psychological stress|stress]], engaging with others, and contributing to life overall.<ref name="MedlinePlus" /> According to the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO), it is a "state of well-being in which the individual realizes their abilities, can [[Coping|cope]] with the normal [[Stress (biology)|stresses]] of life, can [[Work (human activity)|work]] productively and fruitfully, and can contribute to their community".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/major-themes/health-and-well-being |title=Health and Well-Being |website=[[World Health Organization]] |access-date=2023-08-09}}</ref> It likewise determines how an individual handles stress, [[interpersonal relationship]]s, and [[decision-making]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-23 |title=About Mental Health |url=https://www.cdc.gov/mentalhealth/learn/index.htm |access-date=2022-04-11 |work=U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) |language=en-US}}</ref> Mental health includes subjective well-being, perceived [[self-efficacy]], [[autonomy]], [[Competence (law)|competence]], intergenerational dependence, and [[self-actualization]] of one's [[intellect]]ual and emotional potential, among others.<ref name="WHO">{{cite web |url=https://www.who.int/whr/2001/en/whr01_en.pdf?ua=1|title= The world health report 2001 – Mental Health: New Understanding, New Hope |publisher= WHO |access-date= 4 May 2014}}</ref> 

From the perspectives of [[positive psychology]] or [[holism]], mental health is thus not merely the absence of [[mental illness]]. Rather, it is a broader state of well-being that includes an individual's ability to enjoy life and to create a balance between life activities and efforts to achieve [[psychological resilience]].<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Snyder CR, Lopez SJ, Pedrotti JT |title=Positive psychology: the scientific and practical explorations of human strengths |date=2011 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-1-4129-8195-8 |oclc=639574840 }}{{page needed|date=November 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=17 June 2022 |title=Mental health |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mental-health-strengthening-our-response |website=[[World Health Organization]]}}</ref> [[Cultural diversity|Cultural differences]], personal philosophy, subjective assessments, and competing professional theories all affect how one defines "mental health".
{{TOC limit}}

== Mental disorders ==
{{Main article|Mental disorder}}
Mental health, as defined by the [[Public Health Agency of Canada]],<ref>{{cite web |date=2020-10-28 |title=Public Health Agency of Canada |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health.html |access-date=2021-10-02 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref> is an individual's capacity to feel, think, and act in ways to achieve a better [[quality of life]] while respecting personal, social, and cultural boundaries.<ref name="Manwell e007079">{{cite journal | vauthors = Manwell LA, Barbic SP, Roberts K, Durisko Z, Lee C, Ware E, McKenzie K | title = What is mental health? Evidence towards a new definition from a mixed methods multidisciplinary international survey | journal = BMJ Open | volume = 5 | issue = 6 | article-number = e007079 | date = June 2015 | pmid = 26038353 | pmc = 4458606 | doi = 10.1136/bmjopen-2014-007079  | doi-access = free}}</ref> Impairment of any of these is a risk factor for [[mental disorder]]s, or mental illnesses,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Galderisi S, Heinz A, Kastrup M, Beezhold J, Sartorius N | title = A proposed new definition of mental health | language = pl | journal = Psychiatria Polska | volume = 51 | issue = 3 | pages = 407–411 | date = June 2017 | pmid = 28866712 | doi = 10.12740/pp/74145 | doi-access = free }}</ref> which is a component of mental health. In 2019, about 970 million people worldwide suffered from a mental disorder, with [[Anxiety disorder|anxiety]] and [[Depression disorder|depression]] being the most common. The number of people diagnosed with mental disorders has risen significantly over the years.<ref>{{cite web | title = GBD Results | work = Global Health Data Exchange (GHDx) | publisher = Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation. | url = https://vizhub.healthdata.org/gbd-results/ | access-date = 14 May 2022 }}</ref> Mental disorders are defined as health conditions that affect and alter cognitive functioning, emotional responses, and behavior associated with distress and/or impaired functioning.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Manderscheid RW, Ryff CD, Freeman EJ, McKnight-Eily LR, Dhingra S, Strine TW | title = Evolving definitions of mental illness and wellness | journal = Preventing Chronic Disease | volume = 7 | issue = 1 | pages = A19 | date = January 2010 | pmid = 20040234 | pmc = 2811514 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Goldman HH, Grob GN | title = Defining 'mental illness' in mental health policy | journal = Health Affairs | volume = 25 | issue = 3 | pages = 737–49 | date = 2006-05-01 | pmid = 16684739 | doi = 10.1377/hlthaff.25.3.737 }}</ref> The [[ICD-11]] is the global standard used to [[diagnose]], treat, research, and report various mental disorders.<ref>{{Citation| vauthors = Evans SC, Roberts MC |title=''International Classification of Diseases'' ( <SCP> ''ICD'' </SCP> ), Mental and Behavioural Disorders Section |date=2015 |encyclopedia=The Encyclopedia of Clinical Psychology|pages=1–10|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd|language=en|doi=10.1002/9781118625392.wbecp257|isbn=978-1-118-62539-2 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=ICD-11|url=https://icd.who.int/en|access-date=2022-01-18 | work = International Classification of Diseases | publisher = World Health Organization (WHO) }}</ref> In the United States, the [[DSM-5]] is used as the [[Classification of mental disorders|classification system of mental disorders]].<ref name="Regier 92–98">{{cite journal | vauthors = Regier DA, Kuhl EA, Kupfer DJ | title = The DSM-5: Classification and criteria changes | journal = World Psychiatry | volume = 12 | issue = 2 | pages = 92–8 | date = June 2013 | pmid = 23737408 | pmc = 3683251 | doi = 10.1002/wps.20050 }}</ref>

Mental health is associated with a number of lifestyle factors such as diet, exercise, stress, drug use and abuse, social connections, and interactions.<ref name="Regier 92–98"/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Manger S | title = Lifestyle interventions for mental health | journal = Australian Journal of General Practice | volume = 48 | issue = 10 | pages = 670–673 | date = October 2019 | pmid = 31569326 | doi = 10.31128/ajgp-06-19-4964 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Psychiatrists, psychologists, licensed professional clinical counselors, social workers, nurse practitioners, and family physicians can help manage mental illness with treatments such as therapy, counseling, [[medication]], and [[Trauma-informed care]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=What Is the Difference Between Psychologists, Psychiatrists and Social Workers?|url=https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/patients-and-families/psychotherapy-professionals|access-date=2021-11-19| work = American Psychological Association (APA) }}</ref>

== Mental health in the digital age ==

[[Information technology|Digital technology]] has an increasing impact on mental health. Research suggests that constant online connection can increase stress, while digital tools may also expand access to mental-health support for people who cannot easily receive in-person care.<ref name="Aboujaoude2015" />

Research also shows that digital media use can affect adolescents' emotional well-being, social development, and mental health outcomes.<ref name="Nesi2022" />

Cyberbullying and online harassment can worsen mental-health symptoms in children and adolescents. Studies show links between online bullying, depression, and anxiety as well as the long term impacts on individuals.<ref name="Li2024" />

==History==
{{see also|Well-being|Eudaimonia|History of mental disorders}}

=== Early history ===
[[File:Csm 04 fidus-hygiene-kongress 01 ac668fa1b6.jpg|thumb|Highly stylized poster for the [[social hygiene|Hygiene]] Congress in Hamburg, 1912]]
In the mid-19th century, [[William Sweetser]] was the first to coin the term ''mental hygiene'', which can be seen as the precursor to contemporary approaches to work on promoting positive mental health.<ref>{{cite book | veditors = Shook JR |date=April 2012 |chapter=Sweetser, William |pages=1016–1020 |title=Dictionary of Early American Philosophers |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-4411-7140-5 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oOqoAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA1017 }}</ref><ref name=Mandell1995>{{cite web | vauthors = Mandell W |date=1995 |title=Origins of Mental Health, The Realization of an Idea | work = Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health |publisher=Johns Hopkins University |location=Baltimore, MD |access-date=9 June 2015 |url=http://www.jhsph.edu/departments/mental-health/about-us/origins-of-mental-health.html }}</ref> [[Isaac Ray]], the fourth president<ref>{{cite web |title=Isaac Ray Award |url=https://www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists/awards-leadership-opportunities/awards/isaac-ray-award |website=www.psychiatry.org |publisher=American Psychiatric Association|access-date=27 October 2017}}</ref> of the [[American Psychiatric Association]] and one of its founders, further defined mental hygiene as "the art of preserving the mind against all incidents and influences calculated to deteriorate its qualities, impair its energies, or derange its movements.<ref name=Mandell1995/>

In American history, mentally ill patients were thought to be religiously punished. This response persisted through the 1700s, along with the inhumane confinement and stigmatization of such individuals.<ref name="uniteforsight">{{cite web |title=A Brief History of Mental Illness and the U.S. Mental Health Care System |url=http://www.uniteforsight.org/mental-health/module2 |website=www.uniteforsight.org |access-date=2020-05-11 |archive-date=2020-06-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200617230917/http://www.uniteforsight.org/mental-health/module2}}</ref> [[Dorothea Dix]] (1802–1887) was an important figure in the development of the "mental hygiene" movement. Dix was a school teacher who endeavored to help people with mental disorders and to expose the sub-standard conditions into which they were put.<ref name="Barlow1">{{cite book | vauthors = Barlow DH, Durand VM, Steward SH | date = 2009 | title = Abnormal Psychology: An Integrative Approach | edition = Second Canadian | location = Toronto | publisher = Nelson Education | page = 16 | isbn = 978-0-17-644151-7 | url = https://archive.org/details/abnormalpsycholo0000barl/page/n23/mode/2up }}</ref> This became known as the "mental hygiene movement.<ref name=Barlow1/> Before this movement, it was not uncommon that people affected by mental illness would be considerably neglected, often left alone in deplorable conditions without sufficient clothing.<ref name=Barlow1/> From 1840 to 1880, she won the support of the federal government to set up over 30 state psychiatric hospitals; however, they were understaffed, under-resourced, and were accused of violating [[human rights]].<ref name="uniteforsight" />

[[Emil Kraepelin]] in 1896 developed the [[taxonomy (general)|taxonomy]] of mental disorders, which has dominated the field for nearly 80 years. Later, the proposed disease model of abnormality was subjected to analysis and considered normality to be relative to the physical, geographical, and cultural aspects of the defining group.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ebert A, Bär KJ | title = Emil Kraepelin: A pioneer of scientific understanding of psychiatry and psychopharmacology | journal = Indian Journal of Psychiatry | volume = 52 | issue = 2 | pages = 191–2 | date = April 2010 | pmid = 20838510 | pmc = 2927892 | doi = 10.4103/0019-5545.64591 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

At the beginning of the 20th century, [[Clifford Whittingham Beers|Clifford Beers]] founded "Mental Health America – National Committee for Mental Hygiene", after publication of his accounts as a patient in several [[lunatic asylums]], ''A Mind That Found Itself'', in 1908<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Peck A | date = 2013 | title = Mental Health America – Origins | access-date = 9 June 2015 | url = http://www.socialwelfarehistory.com/organizations/mental-health-america-origins | work = The Social Welfare History Project }}</ref><ref name=CliffordBeersClinic>{{cite web |url=http://www.cliffordbeers.org/aboutus.htm |title=About Us | work = Clifford Beers Clinic | location = New Haven, CT |access-date=2007-06-01 |archive-date=2007-04-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070409125103/http://www.cliffordbeers.org/aboutus.htm }}</ref><ref name="The roots of the concept of mental">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bertolote J | title = The roots of the concept of mental health | journal = World Psychiatry | volume = 7 | issue = 2 | pages = 113–6 | date = June 2008 | pmid = 18560478 | pmc = 2408392 | doi = 10.1002/j.2051-5545.2008.tb00172.x }}</ref> and opened the first outpatient mental health [[clinic]] in the United States.<ref name=CliffordBeersClinic/> In the early 20th century, mental illness was increasingly viewed as a public health concern.<ref>{{Cite book |last=May |first=James Vance |date=1922 |title=A Public Health Problem |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/54611 |access-date=2026-04-27}}</ref>

The mental hygiene movement, similar to the [[social hygiene movement]], had at times been associated with advocating [[eugenics]] and the [[sterilisation (medicine)|sterilization]] of those considered too mentally deficient to be assisted into productive work and contented family life.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Jones G |title=Social Hygiene in Twentieth Century Britain |date=1986 |publisher=Croom Helm |location=London |isbn=978-0-7099-1481-5 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=C9IOAAAAQAAJ&q=%27moral+hygiene%27+%27social+hygiene%27+%27mental+hygiene%27+movement | pages = 80–83 }}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia | chapter-url = http://www.faqs.org/childhood/Gr-Im/Hygiene.html | encyclopedia = Encyclopedia of Children and Childhood in History and Society | chapter = Hygiene | vauthors = Wilkie JS | title = Hygiene - Evolving Ideas of Hygiene, Theories of Contagion, Public Hygiene - Encyclopedia of Children and Childhood in History and Society }}</ref> In the post-WWII years, references to mental hygiene were gradually replaced by the term 'mental health' due to its positive aspect that evolves from the treatment of illness to preventive and promotive areas of healthcare.<ref name="The roots of the concept of mental"/>

==== Institutionalization and deinstitutionalization ====
When US government-run hospitals were accused of violating human rights, advocates pushed for [[deinstitutionalization]]: the replacement of federal mental hospitals with [[community mental health service]]s. The closure of state-provisioned psychiatric hospitals was enforced by the [[Community Mental Health Centers Act]] in 1963, which laid out terms under which only patients who posed an imminent danger to others or themselves could be admitted into state facilities.<ref>{{cite report | title=The New York Times New York State Poll, June 2008 | publisher=Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research (ICPSR) | series=CBS News/New York Times Poll Series |id=ICPSR 26164 | date=3 December 2009 | doi=10.3886/icpsr26164.v1 |location=Ann Arbor, MI }}</ref> This was seen as an improvement from previous conditions. However, there remains a debate on the conditions of these community resources.

It has been proven that this transition was beneficial for many patients: there was an increase in overall satisfaction, a better quality of life, and more friendships between patients, all at an affordable cost. This proved to be true only in the circumstance that treatment facilities had enough funding for staff and equipment, as well as proper management.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Knapp M, Beecham J, McDaid D, Matosevic T, Smith M | title = The economic consequences of deinstitutionalisation of mental health services: lessons from a systematic review of European experience | journal = Health & Social Care in the Community | volume = 19 | issue = 2 | pages = 113–25 | date = March 2011 | pmid = 21143545 | doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2524.2010.00969.x | doi-access = free }}</ref> However, this idea is a polarizing issue. Critics of deinstitutionalization argue that poor living conditions prevailed, patients were lonely, and they did not acquire proper medical care in these treatment homes.<ref name="Novella_2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = Novella EJ | title = Mental health care and the politics of inclusion: a social systems account of psychiatric deinstitutionalization | journal = Theoretical Medicine and Bioethics | volume = 31 | issue = 6 | pages = 411–27 | date = December 2010 | pmid = 20711755 | doi = 10.1007/s11017-010-9155-8 }}</ref> Additionally, patients who were moved from state psychiatric care to nursing and residential homes had deficits in crucial aspects of their treatment. Some cases result in the shift of care from health workers to patients' families, where they do not have the proper funding or medical expertise to give proper care.<ref name="Novella_2010" /> On the other hand, patients who are treated in community mental health centers lack sufficient cancer testing, [[vaccination]]s, or regular medical check-ups.<ref name="Novella_2010" />

Other critics of state deinstitutionalization argue that this was simply a transition to "[[transinstitutionalization]], or the idea that prisons and state-provisioned hospitals are interdependent. In other words, patients become inmates. This draws on the Penrose Hypothesis of 1939, which theorized that there was an inverse relationship between prisons' population size and the number of psychiatric hospital beds.<ref name="Schildbach_2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Schildbach S, Schildbach C | title = Criminalization Through Transinstitutionalization: A Critical Review of the Penrose Hypothesis in the Context of Compensation Imprisonment | journal = Frontiers in Psychiatry | volume = 9 | article-number = 534 | date = 25 October 2018 | pmid = 30410452 | pmc = 6209624 | doi = 10.3389/fpsyt.2018.00534 | doi-access = free }}</ref> This means that populations that require psychiatric mental care will transition between institutions, which in this case includes state psychiatric hospitals and criminal justice systems. Thus, a decrease in available psychiatric hospital beds occurred at the same time as an increase in inmates.<ref name="Schildbach_2018" /> Although some are skeptical that this is due to other external factors, others will attribute this conclusion to a lack of empathy for the mentally ill. There is no argument for the social stigmatization of those with mental illnesses; they have been widely marginalized and discriminated against in society.<ref name="uniteforsight" /> In this source, researchers analyze how most compensation prisoners (detainees who are unable or unwilling to pay a fine for petty crimes) are unemployed, homeless, and have an extraordinarily high degree of mental illnesses and [[substance use disorder]]s.<ref name="Schildbach_2018" /> Compensation prisoners then lose prospective job opportunities, face social marginalization, and lack access to resocialization programs, which ultimately facilitate reoffending.<ref name="Schildbach_2018" /> The research sheds light on how the mentally ill—and in this case, the poor—are further punished for certain circumstances that are beyond their control, and that this is a vicious cycle that repeats itself. Thus, prisons embody another state-provisioned mental hospital.

Families of patients, advocates, and mental health professionals still call for an increase in more well-structured community facilities and treatment programs with a higher quality of long-term inpatient resources and care. With this more structured environment, the United States will continue with more access to mental health care and an increase in the overall treatment of the mentally ill.

However, there is still a lack of studies on mental health conditions (MHCs) to raise awareness, knowledge development, and attitudes toward seeking medical treatment for MHCs in Bangladesh. People in rural areas often seek treatment from the traditional healers, and MHCs are sometimes considered a spiritual matter.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Uddin MN, Bhar S, Islam FM | title = An assessment of awareness of mental health conditions and its association with socio-demographic characteristics: a cross-sectional study in a rural district in Bangladesh | journal = BMC Health Services Research | volume = 19 | issue = 1 | article-number = 562 | date = August 2019 | pmid = 31409332 | pmc = 6692949 | doi = 10.1186/s12913-019-4385-6 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Epidemiology ==
{{See also|Prevalence of mental disorders}}
{{owidslider
|start        = 2021
|list         = Template:OWID/share with mental and substance disorders#gallery
|location      = commons
|caption      =
|title        =
|language     =
|file         = [[File:Share-with-mental-and-substance-disorders,World,2021 (cropped).svg|link=|thumb|upright=1.6|Share with mental and substance disorders]]
|startingView = World
}}
[[Mental illnesses]] are more common than [[cancer]], [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetes]], or [[heart disease]]. As of 2021, over 22 percent of all Americans over the age of 18 meet the criteria for having a mental illness.<ref name=nimh>{{cite web |title=Mental Illness |url=https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/statistics/mental-illness |website=National Institute of Mental Health |access-date=13 September 2023}}
</ref> Evidence suggests that 970 million people worldwide have a mental disorder.<ref>{{cite web |date=June 8, 2022 |title=Mental disorders |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mental-disorders |access-date=January 5, 2024 |website=World Health Organization |language=en}}</ref> [[Major depressive disorder|Major depression]] ranks third among the top 10 leading causes of disease worldwide. By 2030, it is predicted to become the leading cause of [[disease]] worldwide.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Bains N, Abdijadid S | chapter = Major Depressive Disorder |date=2023 | chapter-url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559078/ | title = StatPearls |access-date=2024-01-05 |place=Treasure Island (FL) |publisher=StatPearls Publishing |pmid=32644504 }}</ref> Over 700 thousand people commit [[suicide]] every year and around 14 million attempt it.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Suicide prevention |url=https://www.who.int/health-topics/suicide |access-date=January 5, 2024 |website=World Health Organization |language=en}}</ref> A [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) report estimates the global cost of mental illness at nearly $2.5 trillion (two-thirds in indirect costs) in 2010, with a projected increase to over $6 trillion by 2030.<ref>{{cite web | title = The World Health Report 2001: Mental Disorders affect one in four people | date = 28 September 2001 | url = https://www.who.int/whr/2001/media_centre/press_release/en/ |publisher = World Health Organization (WHO) }}</ref>

Evidence from the WHO suggests that nearly half of the world's population is affected by mental illness with an impact on their [[self-esteem]], relationships and ability to function in everyday life.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Storrie K, Ahern K, Tuckett A | title = A systematic review: Students with mental health problems--a growing problem | journal = International Journal of Nursing Practice | volume = 16 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–6 | date = February 2010 | pmid = 20158541 | doi = 10.1111/j.1440-172X.2009.01813.x }}</ref> An individual's emotional health can impact their physical health. Poor mental health can lead to problems such as the inability to make adequate decisions and [[substance use disorder]]s.<ref name="Richards 2010 247">
{{cite journal| vauthors = Richards K, Campenni C, Muse-Burke J |title=Self-care and Well-being in Mental Health Professionals: The Mediating Effects of Self-awareness and Mindfulness|journal=Journal of Mental Health Counseling |date=July 2010 |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=247–264 |doi=10.17744/mehc.32.3.0n31v88304423806}}</ref>

Good mental health can improve life quality whereas poor mental health can worsen it. According to Richards, Campania, & Muse-Burke, "There is growing evidence that is showing emotional abilities are associated with pro-social behaviors such as stress management and physical health."<ref name="Richards 2010 247"/> Their research also concluded that people who lack emotional expression are inclined to anti-social behaviors (e.g., substance use disorder and [[alcohol use disorder]], physical fights, [[vandalism]]), which reflects one's mental health and suppressed emotions.<ref name="Richards 2010 247"/> Adults and children who face mental illness may experience [[social stigma]], which can exacerbate the issues.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Heary C, Hennessy E, Swords L, Corrigan P |title=Stigma towards Mental Health Problems during Childhood and Adolescence: Theory, Research and Intervention Approaches |journal=Journal of Child and Family Studies |date=6 July 2017 |volume=26 |issue=11 |pages=2949–2959 |doi=10.1007/s10826-017-0829-y }}</ref>

=== Global prevalence ===
{{See also|Global mental health|:Category:Mental health by country}}
[[File:Two Continua Model Large.png|thumb|The Two Continua Model of Mental Health and Mental Illness]]
Mental health can be seen as a [[continuum (theory)|continuum]], where an individual's mental health may have many different possible [[Value (ethics)|values]].<ref name=Keyes2002>{{cite journal | vauthors = Keyes CL | title = The mental health continuum: from languishing to flourishing in life | journal = Journal of Health and Social Behavior | volume = 43 | issue = 2 | pages = 207–22 | date = June 2002 | pmid = 12096700 | doi = 10.2307/3090197 | jstor = 3090197 }}</ref> [[Well-being|Mental wellness]] is viewed as a positive attribute; this definition of mental health highlights [[emotional well-being]], the capacity to live a full and [[creativity|creative]] life, and the flexibility to deal with life's inevitable challenges. Some discussions are formulated in terms of contentment or happiness.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Graham MC |title=Facts of Life: ten issues of contentment |date=2014 |publisher=Outskirts Press |isbn=978-1-4787-2259-5 |pages=6–10}}</ref> Many therapeutic systems and self-help books offer methods and philosophies espousing strategies and techniques vaunted as effective for further improving the mental wellness. [[Positive psychology]] is increasingly prominent in mental health.

A [[holistic]] model of mental health generally includes concepts based upon [[anthropological]], [[education]]al, [[psychological]], [[religious]], and [[sociological]] perspectives. There are also models as theoretical perspectives from [[personality psychology|personality]], [[social psychology|social]], [[clinical psychology|clinical]], [[health psychology|health]] and [[developmental psychology]].<ref name=WitmerSweeney>{{cite journal | vauthors = Witmer JM, Sweeny TJ | title = A holistic model for wellness and prevention over the lifespan | journal = Journal of Counseling and Development | volume = 71 | pages = 140–148 | year = 1992 | doi = 10.1002/j.1556-6676.1992.tb02189.x | issue = 2 }}</ref><ref name=HattieMyersSweeney_p354364>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hattie JA, Myers JE, Sweeney TJ | title = A factor structure of wellness: Theory, assessment, analysis and practice | journal = Journal of Counseling and Development | volume = 82 | pages = 354–364 | year = 2004 | doi = 10.1002/j.1556-6678.2004.tb00321.x | issue = 3 }}</ref>

The tripartite model of mental well-being<ref name=Keyes2002/><ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal | vauthors = Joshanloo M |title=Revisiting the Empirical Distinction Between Hedonic and Eudaimonic Aspects of Well-Being Using Exploratory Structural Equation Modeling |journal=Journal of Happiness Studies |volume=17 |issue=5 |pages=2023–2036 |date=23 October 2015 |doi=10.1007/s10902-015-9683-z }}</ref> views mental well-being as encompassing three components of emotional well-being, social well-being, and [[psychological well-being]]. Emotional well-being is defined as having high levels of positive emotions, whereas social and psychological well-being are defined as the presence of psychological and social skills and abilities that contribute to optimal functioning in daily life. The model has received empirical support across cultures.<ref name="ReferenceA"/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bobowik M, Basabe N, Páez D | title = The bright side of migration: hedonic, psychological, and social well-being in immigrants in Spain | journal = Social Science Research | volume = 51 | pages = 189–204 | date = May 2015 | pmid = 25769861 | doi = 10.1016/j.ssresearch.2014.09.011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gallagher MW, Lopez SJ, Preacher KJ | title = The hierarchical structure of well-being | journal = Journal of Personality | volume = 77 | issue = 4 | pages = 1025–50 | date = August 2009 | pmid = 19558444 | pmc = 3865980 | doi = 10.1111/j.1467-6494.2009.00573.x }}</ref> The Mental Health Continuum-Short Form (MHC-SF) is the most widely used scale to measure the tripartite model of mental well-being.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Keyes CL, Wissing M, Potgieter JP, Temane M, Kruger A, van Rooy S | title = Evaluation of the mental health continuum-short form (MHC-SF) in setswana-speaking South Africans | journal = Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy | volume = 15 | issue = 3 | pages = 181–92 | date = May 2008 | pmid = 19115439 | doi = 10.1002/cpp.572 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Joshanloo M, Lamers SM |title=Reinvestigation of the factor structure of the MHC-SF in the Netherlands: Contributions of exploratory structural equation modeling |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=July 2016 |volume=97 |pages=8–12 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2016.02.089 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Joshanloo M | title = A New Look at the Factor Structure of the MHC-SF in Iran and the United States Using Exploratory Structural Equation Modeling | journal = Journal of Clinical Psychology | volume = 72 | issue = 7 | pages = 701–13 | date = July 2016 | pmid = 26990960 | doi = 10.1002/jclp.22287 | hdl = 11343/291078 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

== Demographics ==

=== Adolescent mental health ===
Adolescence is a period when many mental health conditions first appear. Teenagers face major physical, social, and emotional changes that can increase stress and create challenges for their well-being. Research shows that early mental health support helps prevent long-term problems and improves development.<ref name="www.who.int">{{Cite web|title=Adolescent mental health|url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/adolescent-mental-health|access-date=2021-07-08|website=www.who.int|language=en}}</ref>

==== Children and adolescents ====
{{Further| Infant mental health |Mental disorders diagnosed in childhood|Developmental psychopathology}}{{see also|Depression in childhood and adolescence|Adverse childhood experiences}}

Mental health problems in children and adolescents contributed to a global prevalence of 13% in 2015.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Polanczyk |first1=Guilherme V. |last2=Salum |first2=Giovanni A. |last3=Sugaya |first3=Luisa S. |last4=Caye |first4=Arthur |last5=Rohde |first5=Luis A. |date=March 2015 |title=Annual Research Review: A meta-analysis of the worldwide prevalence of mental disorders in children and adolescents |journal=Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry |volume=56 |issue=3 |pages=345–365 |doi=10.1111/jcpp.12381 |pmid=25649325 }}</ref> In 2019, about one in seven of the world's 10–19 year olds experienced a mental health disorder, a total of about 165 million young people.<ref name="www.who.int"/><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mental health|url=https://data.unicef.org/topic/child-health/mental-health/|access-date=2024-05-25| work = The United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF) |language=en}}</ref> Adolescence is a critical and unique phase of development in psychological growth. Children having mental health problems can have adverse outcomes, such as poor school performance, social difficulties, substance abuse, and poor physical health.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Patel |first1=Vikram |last2=Flisher |first2=Alan J |last3=Hetrick |first3=Sarah |last4=McGorry |first4=Patrick |date=April 2007 |title=Mental health of young people: a global public-health challenge |journal=The Lancet |volume=369 |issue=9569 |pages=1302–1313 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(07)60368-7 |pmid=17434406 |bibcode=2007Lanc..369.1302P }}</ref> The adverse effects even extend beyond the children themselves - increased reliance on public sector services and healthcare services, loss [[productivity]] among parents or care-givers, and burden to society.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Beecham |first=Jennifer |date=June 2014 |title=Annual Research Review: Child and adolescent mental health interventions: a review of progress in economic studies across different disorders |journal=Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry |volume=55 |issue=6 |pages=714–732 |doi=10.1111/jcpp.12216 |pmc=4657502 |pmid=24580503}}</ref> More than half of mental health conditions start before a child reaches 20 years of age, with onset occurring in [[adolescence]] much more frequently than it does in early childhood or adulthood. However, pre-school children with early mental health problems are increasing in prevalence in the 21st century.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vasileva |first1=Mira |last2=Graf |first2=Ramona K. |last3=Reinelt |first3=Tilman |last4=Petermann |first4=Ulrike |last5=Petermann |first5=Franz |title=Research review: A meta-analysis of the international prevalence and comorbidity of mental disorders in children between 1 and 7 years |journal=Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry |date=April 2021 |volume=62 |issue=4 |pages=372–381 |doi=10.1111/jcpp.13261 |pmid=32433792 }}</ref>  Many such cases go undetected and untreated.<ref name="www.who.int"/><ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-10-26|title=Mental health statistics: children and young people|url=https://www.mentalhealth.org.uk/statistics/mental-health-statistics-children-and-young-people|access-date=2021-10-05|website=Mental Health Foundation|language=en}}</ref><ref name = "2024Orben">{{cite journal | vauthors = Orben A, Meier A, Dalgleish T, Blakemore S | title = Mechanisms linking social media use to adolescent mental health vulnerability| journal = [[Nature Reviews Psychology]] | date = May 2024 | volume = 3| issue = 6| pages = 407–423| doi =10.1038/s44159-024-00307-y | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McGrath JJ, Al-Hamzawi A, Alonso J, Altwaijri Y, Andrade LH, Bromet EJ, Bruffaerts R, de Almeida JM, Chardoul S, Chiu WT, Degenhardt L, Demler OV, Ferry F, Gureje O, Haro JM, Karam EG, Karam G, Khaled SM, Kovess-Masfety V, Magno M, Medina-Mora ME, Moskalewicz J, Navarro-Mateu F, Nishi D, Plana-Ripoll O, Posada-Villa J, Rapsey C, Sampson NA, Stagnaro JC, Stein DJ, Ten Have M, Torres Y, Vladescu C, Woodruff PW, Zarkov Z, Kessler RC | collaboration = WHO World Mental Health Survey Collaborators | title = Age of onset and cumulative risk of mental disorders: a cross-national analysis of population surveys from 29 countries | journal = The Lancet. Psychiatry | volume = 10 | issue = 9 | pages = 668–681 | date = September 2023 | pmid = 37531964 | doi = 10.1016/S2215-0366(23)00193-1 | pmc = 10529120 }}</ref>

In the United States, in 2021, at least roughly 17.5% of the population (ages 18 and older) were recorded as having a mental illness. The comparison between reports and statistics of mental health issues in newer generations (18–25 years old to 26–49 years old) and the older generation (50 years or older) signifies an increase in mental health issues as only 15% of the older generation reported a mental health issue whereas the newer generations reported 33.7% (18–25) and 28.1% (26–49).<ref name=nimh/>  The role of caregivers for youth with mental health needs is valuable, and caregivers benefit most when they have sufficient psychoeducation and peer support.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yoo A, Kim M, Ross MM, Vaughn-Lee A, Butler B, dosReis S | title = Engaging Caregivers in the Treatment of Youth with Complex Developmental and Mental Health Needs | journal = The Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research | volume = 45 | issue = 3 | pages = 440–453 | date = July 2018 | pmid = 29520663 | doi = 10.1007/s11414-018-9604-0 }}</ref> Depression is one of the leading causes of illness and disability among adolescents.<ref name="www.who.int"/> Suicide is the fourth leading cause of death in 15-19-year-olds.<ref name="www.who.int"/> Exposure to childhood trauma can cause mental health disorders and poor academic achievement.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Larson |first1=Satu |last2=Chapman |first2=Susan |last3=Spetz |first3=Joanne |last4=Brindis |first4=Claire D. |title=Chronic Childhood Trauma, Mental Health, Academic Achievement, and School-Based Health Center Mental Health Services |journal=Journal of School Health |date=September 2017 |volume=87 |issue=9 |pages=675–686 |doi=10.1111/josh.12541 |pmid=28766317 }}</ref> Ignoring mental health conditions in adolescents can impact adulthood.<ref name="Kato_2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kato N, Yanagawa T, Fujiwara T, Morawska A | title = Prevalence of Children's Mental Health Problems and the Effectiveness of Population-Level Family Interventions | journal = Journal of Epidemiology | volume = 25 | issue = 8 | pages = 507–16 | date = 2015 | pmid = 26250791 | pmc = 4517988 | doi = 10.2188/jea.JE20140198 }}</ref> 50% of preschool children show a natural reduction in behavioral problems. The remaining experience long-term consequences.<ref name="Kato_2015" /> It impairs physical and mental health and limits opportunities to live fulfilling lives.<ref name="Kato_2015" /> A result of depression during adolescence and adulthood may be substance abuse.<ref name="Kato_2015" /><ref name="Merikangas_2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Merikangas KR, Nakamura EF, Kessler RC | title = Epidemiology of mental disorders in children and adolescents | journal = Dialogues in Clinical Neuroscience | volume = 11 | issue = 1 | pages = 7–20 | date = 2009 | doi = 10.31887/DCNS.2009.11.1/krmerikangas | pmid = 19432384 | pmc = 2807642 }}</ref> The average age of onset is between 11 and 14 years for depressive disorders.<ref name="Merikangas_2009" /> Only approximately 25% of children with behavioral problems refer to medical services.<ref name="Kato_2015" /> The majority of children go untreated.<ref name="Kato_2015" /> A global study of more than 275,000 adolescents aged 12–17 years across 82 countries found that 14% had experienced suicidal thoughts and 9% had anxiety over a 12-month period; adolescents with fewer peer and parental supports and greater exposure to peer conflict, victimisation, and loneliness were at higher risk, and 36 of the 82 countries studied had no specific national mental health policy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Teen mental health study |url=https://www.arc.gov.au/news-and-publications/media/teen-mental-health-study |website=Australian Research Council |date=8 September 2021 |access-date=16 March 2026}}</ref>

=== Mental health and Dementia ===
Mental health conditions are common in people living with dementia.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kwon |first1=Chan-Young |last2=Lee |first2=Boram |date=2021-10-21 |title=Prevalence of Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia in Community-Dwelling Dementia Patients: A Systematic Review |journal=Frontiers in Psychiatry |volume=12 |article-number=741059 |doi=10.3389/fpsyt.2021.741059 |doi-access=free |pmc=8566725 |pmid=34744832}}</ref> Depression and anxiety frequently occur alongside cognitive decline,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leung |first1=Dara K.Y. |last2=Chan |first2=Wai Chi |last3=Spector |first3=Aimee |last4=Wong |first4=Gloria H.Y. |title=Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and apathy symptoms across dementia stages: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry |date=September 2021 |volume=36 |issue=9 |pages=1330–1344 |doi=10.1002/gps.5556 |pmid=33905138 |url=https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10127275/ }}</ref> and can worsen day‑to‑day functioning and quality of life.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tonga |first1=Johanne B. |last2=Eilertsen |first2=Dag-Erik |last3=Solem |first3=Ingrid K. Ledel |last4=Arnevik |first4=Espen A. |last5=Korsnes |first5=Maria S. |last6=Ulstein |first6=Ingun D. |date=2020-01-01 |title=Effect of Self-Efficacy on Quality of Life in People With Mild Cognitive Impairment and Mild Dementia: The Mediating Roles of Depression and Anxiety |journal=American Journal of Alzheimer's Disease & Other Dementias |volume=35 |article-number=1533317519885264 |doi=10.1177/1533317519885264 |pmc=10623983 |pmid=31916847}}</ref> People with dementia who experience co‑morbid depression or anxiety are at increased risk of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and death by suicide, particularly in the earlier stages of dementia.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Medeisyte |first1=Radvile |last2=Nuzum |first2=Eleanor |last3=John |first3=Amber |last4=Tsipa |first4=Anastasia |last5=Fearn |first5=Caroline |last6=Charlesworth |first6=Georgina |last7=Crutch |first7=Sebastian J. |last8=El Baou |first8=Céline |last9=Stewart |first9=Gavin R. |last10=Kurana |first10=Suman |last11=Brotherhood |first11=Emilie V. |last12=Flanagan |first12=Katie |last13=Salmoiraghi |first13=Alberto |last14=Kerti |first14=Amy |last15=Stott |first15=Joshua |last16=Desai |first16=Roopal |title=Risk of suicide in people living with dementia and comorbid mental health conditions: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=Journal of Affective Disorders |date=June 2025 |volume=379 |pages=835–844 |doi=10.1016/j.jad.2025.03.075 |pmid=40097114 }}</ref>

Some groups appear to have an even higher likelihood of developing mood problems. For example, frontotemporal dementia is often associated with early behavioural and emotional changes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wittenberg |first1=Dana |last2=Possin |first2=Katherine L. |last3=Rascovsky |first3=Katya |last4=Rankin |first4=Katherine P. |last5=Miller |first5=Bruce L. |last6=Kramer |first6=Joel H. |date=March 2008 |title=The Early Neuropsychological and Behavioral Characteristics of Frontotemporal Dementia |journal=Neuropsychology Review |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=91–102 |doi=10.1007/s11065-008-9056-z |pmc=3000668 |pmid=18311522}}</ref> and people with young‑onset dementia (where symptoms begin before age 65) may be more vulnerable to depression and anxiety<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Jessica D. |last2=Henley |first2=Susie M.D. |last3=Suárez-González |first3=Aida |title=A systematic review of the prevalence of depression, anxiety, and apathy in frontotemporal dementia, atypical and young-onset Alzheimer's disease, and inherited dementia |journal=International Psychogeriatrics |date=September 2023 |volume=35 |issue=9 |pages=457–476 |doi=10.1017/S1041610220001118 |pmid=32684177 }}</ref> because of the impact on employment,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Page |first1=Laura |last2=Meredith |first2=Pamela |last3=O’Reilly |first3=Maria |last4=Donohue |first4=Genevieve |last5=Stanley |first5=Mandy |title=Understanding employee experiences of developing younger onset dementia within the workplace: A scoping review |journal=Work |date=January 2025 |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=24–60 |doi=10.3233/WOR-230469 |pmid=39177636 }}</ref>  identity,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tang |first1=Xueting |last2=Wang |first2=Junqiao |last3=Wu |first3=Bei |last4=Navarra |first4=Ann-Margaret |last5=Cui |first5=Xiaoyan |last6=Wang |first6=Jing |date=2023-11-01 |title=Lived experiences of maintaining self-identity among persons living with young-onset dementia: A qualitative meta-synthesis |journal=Dementia |volume=22 |issue=8 |pages=1776–1798 |doi=10.1177/14713012231193547 |pmid=37646673 }}</ref> and family roles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Popok |first1=Paula J |last2=Reichman |first2=Mira |last3=LeFeber |first3=Lisa |last4=Grunberg |first4=Victoria A |last5=Bannon |first5=Sarah M |last6=Vranceanu |first6=Ana-Maria |date=2022-04-20 |title=One Diagnosis, Two Perspectives: Lived Experiences of Persons With Young-Onset Dementia and Their Care-Partners |journal=The Gerontologist |volume=62 |issue=9 |pages=1311–1323 |doi=10.1093/geront/gnac050 |pmc=9579459 |pmid=35442443}}</ref>

Mental health conditions in people living with dementia are often under-recognised and undertreated.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The interface between dementia and mental health |url=https://www.mentalhealth.org.uk/explore-mental-health/publications/interface-between-dementia-and-mental-health |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=www.mentalhealth.org.uk |language=en}}</ref> Untreated depression and anxiety can contribute to distress, behavioural changes, greater care needs and an increased risk of admission to long‑term care.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Feast |first1=Alexandra |last2=Moniz-Cook |first2=Esme |last3=Stoner |first3=Charlotte |last4=Charlesworth |first4=Georgina |last5=Orrell |first5=Martin |title=A systematic review of the relationship between behavioral and psychological symptoms (BPSD) and caregiver well-being |journal=International Psychogeriatrics |date=November 2016 |volume=28 |issue=11 |pages=1761–1774 |doi=10.1017/S1041610216000922 |pmid=27345942 }}</ref> However, it is not inevitable that people with dementia will experience mood problems.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Amponsem |first1=Sheriffa |last2=Wolverson |first2=Emma |last3=Clarke |first3=Chris |title=The meaning and experience of hope by people living with dementia as expressed through poetry |journal=Dementia |date=January 2023 |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=125–143 |doi=10.1177/14713012221137469 |pmid=36350191 }}</ref> When symptoms occur, they can be assessed as for those living without dementia. Non‑drug approaches—such as psychological therapies,<ref name=overv>{{Cite web |date=2018-06-20 |title=Overview {{!}} Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers |url=https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97 |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=www.nice.org.uk}}</ref> social engagement,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Papavasiliou |first1=Evie |last2=Marshall |first2=Jessica |last3=Allan |first3=Louise |last4=Bradbury |first4=Katherine |last5=Fox |first5=Chris |last6=Hawkes |first6=Matthew |last7=Irvine |first7=Anne |last8=Moniz-Cook |first8=Esme |last9=Pick |first9=Aimee |last10=Polley |first10=Marie |last11=Rathbone |first11=Amy |last12=Reeve |first12=Joanne |last13=Robinson |first13=Dame Louise |last14=Rook |first14=George |last15=Sadler |first15=Euan |date=2025 |title=Reimagining Dementia Care: A Complex Intervention Systematic Review on Optimising Social Prescribing (SP) for People Living With Dementia (PLWD) in the United Kingdom |journal=Health Expectations |language=en |volume=28 |issue=3 |article-number=e70289 |doi=10.1111/hex.70289 |doi-access=free |pmid=40356285 |pmc=12069811 }}</ref> and activity‑based interventions<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Erin Rachel |last2=Aggar |first2=Christina |last3=Bissett |first3=Michelle |title=Nonpharmacological tactile activity interventions for reducing behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia in the acute hospital setting: An integrative review |journal=Journal of Clinical Nursing |date=December 2023 |volume=32 |issue=23–24 |pages=7970–7978 |doi=10.1111/jocn.16891 |pmid=37795921 }}</ref> are recommended as first‑line treatments, with medication reserved for specific situations.<ref name=overv/>

Research also suggests that mental health difficulties earlier in life may be linked to later dementia risk.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kuring |first1=J. K. |last2=Mathias |first2=J. L. |last3=Ward |first3=L. |title=Prevalence of Depression, Anxiety and PTSD in People with Dementia: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis |journal=Neuropsychology Review |date=December 2018 |volume=28 |issue=4 |pages=393–416 |doi=10.1007/s11065-018-9396-2 |pmid=30536144 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stafford |first1=Jean |last2=Chung |first2=Wing Tung |last3=Sommerlad |first3=Andrew |last4=Kirkbride |first4=James B. |last5=Howard |first5=Robert |date=2022 |title=Psychiatric disorders and risk of subsequent dementia: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies |journal=International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry |language=en |volume=37 |issue=5 |article-number=gps.5711 |doi=10.1002/gps.5711 |pmid=35460299 |pmc=9325434 }}</ref> Long‑term cohort studies have found that depression in midlife is associated with a higher likelihood of developing dementia decades later.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frank |first1=Philipp |last2=Singh-Manoux |first2=Archana |last3=Pentti |first3=Jaana |last4=Batty |first4=G David |last5=Sommerlad |first5=Andrew |last6=Steptoe |first6=Andrew |last7=Livingston |first7=Gill |last8=Howard |first8=Robert |last9=Kivimäki |first9=Mika |title=Specific midlife depressive symptoms and long-term dementia risk: a 23-year UK prospective cohort study |journal=The Lancet Psychiatry |date=February 2026 |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=100–111 |doi=10.1016/S2215-0366(25)00331-1 |pmid=41412145 }}</ref>

=== Homeless population ===
{{Further| Homelessness and mental health}}
Mental illness is thought to be highly prevalent among homeless populations, though access to proper diagnoses is limited. An article written by Lisa Goodman and her colleagues summarized Smith's research into PTSD in homeless single women and mothers in St. Louis, Missouri, which found that 53% of the respondents met diagnostic criteria, and which describes homelessness as a risk factor for mental illness.<ref name="Homelessness as psychological traum">{{cite journal|vauthors=Goodman L, Saxe L, Harvey M|date=November 1991|title=Homelessness as psychological trauma. Broadening perspectives|journal=The American Psychologist|volume=46|issue=11|pages=1219–25|doi=10.1037/0003-066x.46.11.1219|pmid=1772159}}</ref> At least two commonly reported symptoms of psychological trauma, social disaffiliation and learned helplessness are highly prevalent among homeless individuals and families.<ref name="Hwang">{{cite journal|vauthors=Hwang SW, Tolomiczenko G, Kouyoumdjian FG, Garner RE|date=November 2005|title=Interventions to improve the health of the homeless: a systematic review|journal=American Journal of Preventive Medicine|volume=29|issue=4|pages=311–9|doi=10.1016/j.amepre.2005.06.017|pmid=16242595}}</ref>

While mental illness is prevalent, people infrequently receive appropriate care.<ref name="Homelessness as psychological traum" /> Case management linked to other services is an effective care approach for improving symptoms in people experiencing homelessness.<ref name="Hwang" /> Case management reduced admission to hospitals, and it reduced substance use by those with substance abuse problems more than typical care.<ref name="Hwang" />

=== Immigrants and refugees ===
{{See also|Mental health of refugees}}
States that produce refugees are sites of social upheaval, civil war, even genocide.<ref name="Miller_2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Miller A, Hess JM, Bybee D, Goodkind JR | title = Understanding the mental health consequences of family separation for refugees: Implications for policy and practice | journal = The American Journal of Orthopsychiatry | volume = 88 | issue = 1 | pages = 26–37 | date = 2018 | pmid = 28617002 | pmc = 5732089 | doi = 10.1037/ort0000272 }}</ref> Most refugees experience trauma. It can be in the form of torture, sexual assault, family fragmentation, and death of loved ones.<ref name="Miller_2018" /><ref name="Sangalang_2019">{{cite journal |last1=Sangalang |first1=Cindy C. |last2=Becerra |first2=David |last3=Mitchell |first3=Felicia M. |last4=Lechuga-Peña |first4=Stephanie |last5=Lopez |first5=Kristina |last6=Kim |first6=Isok |title=Trauma, Post-Migration Stress, and Mental Health: A Comparative Analysis of Refugees and Immigrants in the United States |journal=Journal of Immigrant and Minority Health |date=October 2019 |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=909–919 |doi=10.1007/s10903-018-0826-2 |pmid=30244330 }}</ref>

Refugees and immigrants experience [[psychosocial stress]]ors after resettlement.<ref name="Bustamante_2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bustamante LH, Cerqueira RO, Leclerc E, Brietzke E | title = Stress, trauma, and posttraumatic stress disorder in migrants: a comprehensive review | journal = Revista Brasileira de Psiquiatria | volume = 40 | issue = 2 | pages = 220–225 | date = 2017-10-19 | pmid = 29069252 | pmc = 6900760 | doi = 10.1590/1516-4446-2017-2290 }}</ref> These include discrimination, lack of economic stability, and social isolation causing emotional distress. For example, not far into the 1900s, campaigns targeting Japanese immigrants were being formed that inhibited their ability to participate in U.S. life, painting them as a threat to the American working-class. They were subject to prejudice and slandered by American media as well as anti-Japanese legislation being implemented.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The U.S. Mainland: Growth and Resistance {{!}} Japanese {{!}} Immigration and Relocation in U.S. History {{!}} Classroom Materials at the Library of Congress |url=https://www.loc.gov/classroom-materials/immigration/japanese/the-us-mainland-growth-and-resistance/ |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=Library of Congress | location = Washington, D.C. USA }}</ref><ref name="Miller_2018" /><ref name="Sangalang_2019" /> For refugees family reunification can be one of the primary needs to improve quality of life.<ref name="Miller_2018" /> Post-migration trauma is a cause of depressive disorders and psychological distress for immigrants.<ref name="Miller_2018" /><ref name="Sangalang_2019" /><ref name="Bustamante_2017" />

===<span class="anchor" id="Psychiatric social work"></span>Mental health in social work===
{{Further| Social work}}{{see also|Clinical social work}}
[[Social work]] in mental health, also called psychiatric social work, is a process where an individual in a setting is helped to attain freedom from overlapping internal and external problems (social and economic situations, family and other relationships, the physical and organizational environment, psychiatric symptoms, etc.). It aims for harmony, [[quality of life]], self-actualization and personal adaptation across all systems. Psychiatric social workers are [[mental health professional]]s that can assist patients and their family members in coping with both mental health issues and various economic or social problems caused by mental illness or psychiatric dysfunctions and to attain improved mental health and well-being. They are vital members of the treatment teams in Departments of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences in hospitals. They are employed in both outpatient and inpatient settings of a hospital, nursing homes, state and local governments, substance use clinics, correctional facilities, health care services, private practice, etc.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Francis AP |title=Social Work in Mental Health: Contexts and Theories for Practice |date=2014 |publisher=SAGE Publications India |isbn=978-93-5150-116-9 }}{{page needed|date=November 2019}}</ref>

In the United States, social workers provide most of the mental health services. According to government sources, 60 percent of mental health professionals are [[Clinical social work|clinically trained social workers]], 10 percent are [[psychiatrist]]s, 23 percent are [[psychologist]]s, and 5 percent are [[psychiatric nurse]]s.<ref>National Association of Social Workers, 2011</ref>

Mental health social workers in Japan have professional knowledge of health and welfare and skills essential for person's well-being. Their social work training enables them as a professional to carry out Consultation assistance for mental disabilities and their social reintegration; Consultation regarding the rehabilitation of the victims; Advice and guidance for post-discharge residence and re-employment after hospitalized care, for major life events in regular life, money and self-management and other relevant matters to equip them to adapt in daily life. Social workers provide individual home visits for mentally ill and do welfare services available, with specialized training a range of procedural services are coordinated for home, workplace and school. In an administrative relationship, Psychiatric social workers provides consultation, leadership, conflict management and work direction. Psychiatric social workers who provides assessment and psychosocial interventions function as a clinician, counselor and municipal staff of the health centers.<ref>{{cite web |title=精神保健福祉士の受験資格を取得するための養成課程 |trans-title=Psychiatric Social Worker Training Course |website=Japan College of Social Work |url=http://www.jcsw.ac.jp/faculty/tsushin/seishin/index.html |language=ja |access-date=2016-02-10 |archive-date=2017-10-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171026214336/http://www.jcsw.ac.jp/faculty/tsushin/seishin/index.html }}</ref>

== Risk factors and causes ==
{{main|Causes of mental disorders}}

There are many things that can contribute to mental health problems, including biological factors, genetic factors, environment, life experiences (such as [[psychological trauma]] or [[Domestic violence|abuse]]), and a [[Family history (medicine)|family history]] of mental health problems.<ref name="mentalhealth.gov"/>

=== Biological ===
According to [[National Institutes of Health|the National Institute of Health]] Curriculum Supplement Series book, most scientists believe that changes in neurotransmitters can cause mental illnesses. In the section "The Biology of Mental Illnesses" the issue is explained in detail, "...there may be disruptions in the neurotransmitters dopamine, glutamate, and norepinephrine in individuals who have schizophrenia".<ref>{{cite book |title=NIH Curriculum Supplement Series [Internet] |date=2007 |publisher=National Institutes of Health |chapter-url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK20369/ |chapter=Information about Mental Illness and the Brain }}</ref>

=== Demographic ===
Gender, age, ethnicity, life expectancy, longevity, population density, and community diversity are all demographic characteristics that can increase the risk and severity of mental disorders.<ref name=Lancet1>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lund C, Brooke-Sumner C, Baingana F, Baron EC, Breuer E, Chandra P, Haushofer J, Herrman H, Jordans M, Kieling C, Medina-Mora ME, Morgan E, Omigbodun O, Tol W, Patel V, Saxena S | title = Social determinants of mental disorders and the Sustainable Development Goals: a systematic review of reviews | journal = The Lancet. Psychiatry | volume = 5 | issue = 4 | pages = 357–369 | date = April 2018 | pmid = 29580610 | doi = 10.1016/S2215-0366(18)30060-9 }}</ref>

===Disability===
[[File:The prevalence of mental illness is higher in more unequal rich countries.jpg|thumb|The prevalence of mental illness is higher in more [[economic inequality|economically unequal]] countries.|alt=|275x275px]]Emotional mental disorders are a leading cause of disabilities worldwide. Investigating the degree and severity of untreated emotional mental disorders throughout the world is a top priority of the [[World Mental Health survey initiative|World Mental Health]] (WMH) survey initiative,<ref>{{cite web |title=The World Mental Health Survey Initiative |url=http://www.hcp.med.harvard.edu/wmh/ |publisher=Harvard Medical School |access-date=23 January 2016 }}</ref> which was created in 1998 by the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Wang PS, Aguilar-Gaxiola S, Alonso J, Angermeyer MC, Borges G, Bromet EJ, Bruffaerts R, de Girolamo G, de Graaf R, Gureje O, Haro JM, Karam EG, Kessler RC, Kovess V, Lane MC, Lee S, Levinson D, Ono Y, Petukhova M, Posada-Villa J, Seedat S, Wells JE | title = Use of mental health services for anxiety, mood, and substance disorders in 17 countries in the WHO world mental health surveys | journal = Lancet | volume = 370 | issue = 9590 | pages = 841–50 | date = September 2007 | pmid = 17826169 | pmc = 2847360 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(07)61414-7 }}</ref> "[[Neuropsychiatric]] disorders are the leading causes of disability worldwide, accounting for 37% of all healthy life years lost through disease. These disorders are most destructive to low and middle-income countries due to their inability to provide their citizens with proper aid. Despite modern treatment and rehabilitation for emotional mental health disorders, "even economically advantaged societies have competing priorities and budgetary constraints".

===Unhappy marriage and divorce ===
Unhappily married couples suffer 3–25 times the risk of developing clinical depression, leading to [[divorce]].<ref>{{Cite journal | vauthors = Gray TD, Hawrilenko M, Cordova JV |date=2019 |title=Randomized Controlled Trial of the Marriage Checkup: Depression Outcomes |journal=Journal of Marital and Family Therapy |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=507–522 |doi=10.1111/jmft.12411 |pmid=31584721 |url=https://arammu.com/assets/research/MC%20Depression%20Outcomes.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fink BC, Shapiro AF | title = Coping Mediates the Association Between Marital Instability and Depression, but Not Marital Satisfaction and Depression | journal = Couple & Family Psychology | volume = 2 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–13 | date = March 2013 | pmid = 25032063 | pmc = 4096140 | doi = 10.1037/a0031763 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | vauthors = Goldfarb MR, Trudel G |date=2019 |title=Marital quality and depression: a review |journal=Marriage & Family Review |volume=55 |issue=8 |pages=737–763 |doi=10.1080/01494929.2019.1610136 }}</ref> Studies found that divorce and separation increases chances of an individual encountering depression, anxiety, substance abuse issues, insomnia, and financial hardship.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Richards |first1=M. |last2=Hardy |first2=R. |last3=Wadsworth |first3=M. |date=September 1997 |title=The effects of divorce and separation on mental health in a national UK birth cohort |journal=Psychological Medicine |volume=27 |issue=5 |pages=1121–1128 |doi=10.1017/s003329179700559x |pmid=9300516}}</ref>  Divorce and unhappy married couples not only affect the mental health of both the parents, but particularly the children of a separated home. Children of divorced parents engage in early sexual behavior, academic difficulties, substance abuse, depressive moods, and an increased chance of living in poverty due to family instability.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=D'Onofrio |first1=Brian |last2=Emery |first2=Robert |title=Parental divorce or separation and children's mental health |journal=World Psychiatry |date=February 2019 |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=100–101 |doi=10.1002/wps.20590 |pmid=30600636 |pmc=6313686 }}</ref>

=== Stress ===
[[File:Inspired by 'Dementia Friends' training at @mcrmuseum last week (14650851663).jpg|thumb|Dementia Friends training]]
The [[Centre for Addiction and Mental Health]] discusses how a certain amount of stress is a normal part of daily life. Small doses of stress help people meet deadlines, be prepared for presentations, be productive and arrive on time for important events. However, long-term stress can become harmful. When stress becomes overwhelming and prolonged, the risks for mental health problems and medical problems increase."<ref>{{Cite web|title=20131 Stress|url=https://www.camh.ca/en/health-info/mental-illness-and-addiction-index/stress|access-date=2020-11-13|website=CAMH|language=en-CA}}</ref> Also on that note, some studies have found language to deteriorate mental health and even harm humans.<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors = Vey JS, Love H |date=2020-07-13|title=Recognizing that words have the power to harm, we commit to using more just language to describe places|url=https://www.brookings.edu/blog/the-avenue/2020/07/13/recognizing-that-words-have-the-power-to-harm-we-commit-to-using-more-just-language-to-describe-places/|access-date=2021-05-09|website=Brookings|language=en-US}}</ref>

The impact of a stressful environment has also been highlighted by different models. Mental health has often been understood from the lens of the [[Diathesis–stress model|vulnerability-stress model]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Monroe SM, Simons AD | title = Diathesis-stress theories in the context of life stress research: implications for the depressive disorders | journal = Psychological Bulletin | volume = 110 | issue = 3 | pages = 406–425 | date = November 1991 | pmid = 1758917 | doi = 10.1037/0033-2909.110.3.406 }}</ref> In that context, stressful situations may contribute to a preexisting vulnerability to negative mental health outcomes being realized. On the other hand, the [[Differential susceptibility|differential susceptibility hypothesis]] suggests that mental health outcomes are better explained by an increased sensitivity to the environment than by vulnerability.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Belsky J, Pluess M | title = Beyond diathesis stress: differential susceptibility to environmental influences | journal = Psychological Bulletin | volume = 135 | issue = 6 | pages = 885–908 | date = November 2009 | pmid = 19883141 | doi = 10.1037/a0017376 | bibcode = 2009PsycB.135..885B }}</ref> For example, it was found that children scoring higher on observer-rated environmental sensitivity often derive more harm from low-quality parenting, but also more benefits from high-quality parenting than those children scoring lower on that measure.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lionetti F, Aron EN, Aron A, Klein DN, Pluess M | title = Observer-rated environmental sensitivity moderates children's response to parenting quality in early childhood | journal = Developmental Psychology | volume = 55 | issue = 11 | pages = 2389–2402 | date = November 2019 | pmid = 31414847 | pmc = 7565718 | doi = 10.1037/dev0000795 }}</ref>

===Unemployment===
[[Unemployment]] has been shown to hurt an individual's emotional well-being, [[self-esteem]], and more broadly their mental health. Increasing unemployment has been shown to have a significant impact on mental health, predominantly depressive disorders.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Extremera N, Rey L | title = Attenuating the Negative Impact of Unemployment: The Interactive Effects of Perceived Emotional Intelligence and Well-Being on Suicide Risk | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 11 | issue = 9 | article-number = e0163656 | date = 29 September 2016 | pmid = 27685996 | pmc = 5042532 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0163656 | bibcode = 2016PLoSO..1163656E | doi-access = free }}</ref> This is an important consideration when reviewing the triggers for mental health disorders in any population survey.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Unemployment impairs mental health: Meta-analysis| vauthors = Paul KI, Moser K |date = 2009|journal = Journal of Vocational Behavior|doi = 10.1016/j.jvb.2009.01.001|volume=74|issue = 3|pages=264–282}}</ref> According to a 2009 meta-analysis by Paul and Moser, countries with high income inequality and poor unemployment protections experience worse mental health outcomes among the unemployed.<ref>{{Cite journal | vauthors = Pappas S | title = The toll of job loss. | journal = Monitor on Psychology | date = 2020 | volume = 51 | issue = 7 | pages = 51–61 |url= https://www.apa.org/monitor/2020/10/toll-job-loss |access-date=2023-11-26 }}</ref>

=== Environmental factors ===
