During the [[medieval period]] in the West, [[Christian philosophy|Christian thinkers]] associated well-being with spiritual [[salvation]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Hyland|Jackson|Rothery|2025|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=MPCIEQAAQBAJ&pg=PA2 2–3]}} | {{harvnb|McMahon|2013|pp=254–255}} }}</ref> [[Augustine]] (354–430 CE) argued that humans are not fully in control of their well-being and instead depend on [[divine grace]]. He maintained that true happiness is achievable only in the [[afterlife]].<ref>{{harvnb|McMahon|2013|pp=255–256}}</ref> [[Thomas Aquinas]] (1225–1274 CE) similarly emphasized the role of the divine, proposing that a [[Beatific vision|beatific vision of God]] is the highest form of well-being.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|McMahon|2013|p=255}} | {{harvnb|Wieland|2002|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=PtLyH02x60MC&pg=PA59 59]}} | {{harvnb|Zagzebski|2004|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=GbcuCf9TlDgC&pg=PA350 350]}} }}</ref> A religion-focused conception of well-being is also found in the [[Islamic philosophy|Islamic tradition]] and the teachings of the [[Quran]], which asserts that material pleasures are temporary and that genuine well-being depends on religious faith and complete dedication to [[Allah]].<ref>{{harvnb|Joshanloo|2017|pp=115–118, 130}}</ref>

=== Modern and contemporary ===
In the [[modern period]], [[secularization]] and [[scientific progress]] shifted the focus from religious theories to [[Naturalism (philosophy)|naturalistic]] explanations, particularly starting in the late 17th century with the [[Age of Enlightenment]]. [[Voltaire]] (1694–1778), [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] (1712–1778), [[Denis Diderot]] (1713–1784), [[Adam Smith]] (1723–1790), and [[François-Jean de Chastellux]] (1734–1788) rejected a religious focus on otherworldly well-being, emphasizing instead the pursuit of earthly happiness through reason, empirical inquiry, and social progress.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Hyland|Jackson|Rothery|2025|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=MPCIEQAAQBAJ&pg=PA3 3]}} | {{harvnb|McMahon|2013|p=257}} | {{harvnb|Stoll|2014|pp=16–18}} | {{harvnb|Michalos|Weijers|2017|pp=46–49}} }}</ref>

[[File:Jeremy Bentham by Henry William Pickersgill detail.jpg|thumb|upright=.8|alt=Oil painting of a man with long gray hair in a formal attire|[[Jeremy Bentham]] proposed the [[felicific calculus]] as a method to measure, compare, and aggregate degrees of pleasure and pain.<ref name="multiref_harvnb_stoll">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stoll|2014|pp=18–20}} | {{harvnb|Michalos|Weijers|2017|pp=41, 49–51}} | {{harvnb|McMahon|2013|pp=260–261}} }}</ref>]]

As the father of [[classical utilitarianism]], [[Jeremy Bentham]] (1748–1832) proposed the [[felicific calculus]] as a method to measure, compare, and aggregate degrees of pleasure and pain, considering factors such as their intensity and duration. He also suggested a direct link between well-being and [[Ethics|right action]], arguing that individuals and governments should promote "the greatest happiness of the greatest number". His student [[John Stuart Mill]] (1806–1873) modified Bentham's idea, proposing that the contribution to well-being depends on the quality of the pleasure. He held that higher pleasures of the mind are more valuable than lower pleasures of the body, even if they have the same intensity and duration.<ref name="multiref_harvnb_stoll" /> [[Thomas Carlyle]] (1795–1881) rejected the utilitarian pursuit of happiness and the individualist market economy associated with Adam Smith, arguing instead that a sense of community and meaningful work are essential to well-being.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Michalos|Weijers|2017|p=51}} | {{harvnb|Stoll|2014|p=20}} }}</ref>

The emergence of [[psychology]] as an empirical science prompted research into the internal factors of well-being, such as [[William James]]'s (1842–1910) introspective research into the connection between happiness and [[religious experience]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stoll|2014|p=22}} | {{harvnb|Hyland|Jackson|Rothery|2025|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=MPCIEQAAQBAJ&pg=PA3 3]}} }}</ref> The [[psychoanalytic theory]] of [[Sigmund Freud]] (1856–1939) characterized the pursuit of pleasure and the reduction of tension as central aims of life.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stoll|2014|p=22}} | {{harvnb|Huta|2013|p=203}} }}</ref> His early collaborator [[Carl Jung]] (1875–1961) explored how well-being depends on [[Individuation#Carl Jung|individuation]] as a form of psychological growth in which [[Consciousness|conscious]] and [[Unconscious mind|unconscious]] aspects are integrated.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Milton|2018|pp=154–155}} | {{harvnb|Galvin|2018|p=7}} }}</ref>

After the [[Second World War]], researchers began conducting large-scale [[Survey (human research)|surveys]] and proposing broad social indicators to track well-being within nations and in cross-national comparisons.<ref>{{harvnb|Stoll|2014|pp=24–24}}</ref> Based on their results, [[Richard Easterlin]] (1926–2024) formulated the [[Easterlin paradox]]{{em dash}}the observation that richer individuals in a nation report higher happiness than poorer ones, although the average happiness of the population does not increase as the nation's average income rises.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Alexandrova|2017|pp=xvii–xviii}} | {{harvnb|Easterlin|O'Connor|2022|pp=[https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007/978-3-319-57365-6_184-2 1–25]}} | {{harvnb|Stoll|2014|p=25}} }}</ref>

Various models of well-being were proposed in the second half of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century, including [[Ed Diener]]'s (1946–2021) tripartite model of subjective well-being, [[Carol Ryff]]'s (born 1950) [[six-factor model of psychological well-being]], and [[Martin Seligman]]'s (born 1942) [[PERMA model]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Barker|2019|loc=[https://books.google.com/books?id=E_7EDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA1944 § Psychological theories of Wellbeing]}} | {{harvnb|Gallagher|Lopez|Preacher|2009|pp=1025–1027}} }}</ref> [[Derek Parfit]] (1942–2017) analyzed traditional theories of well-being and introduced the influential distinction between hedonism, desire theories, and objective list theories.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Tiberius|2015|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=uvzVBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA167 167]}} | {{harvnb|Smith|2020|pp=160–161}} }}</ref>

Another key development was the emergence of [[positive psychology]] in the late 1990s, focusing on human flourishing and optimal functioning in contrast to the traditional emphasis of psychological research on illness and dysfunction.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Allison|2024|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ALklEQAAQBAJ&pg=PA1593 1593]}} | {{harvnb|Stoll|2014|p=26}} }}</ref> The 20th and 21st centuries also saw growing interest in the relation between well-being, [[economy]], and [[public policy]], as governments and international organizations began integrating research on well-being into political decision-making.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stoll|2014|pp=25–27}} | {{harvnb|Hyland|Jackson|Rothery|2025|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=MPCIEQAAQBAJ&pg=PA4 4]}} }}</ref>
